events.title: The spring under the shoulder of the hill fails
events.body: The spring that fed Neachdan's valley thins through a wet season and fails by the dark of the year, leaving four households to carry water a mile and a half by skin. The valley meets and chooses to sink a well of its own.

events.title: Neachdan chosen to sink the well
events.body: The households of the failed spring choose Neachdan, the best splitter of stone among them, to dig a new well. He has already gone to mark the shaft while the others are still weighing whether the old spring might return.

events.title: Neachdan's hands split at the knuckle
events.body: Through the dead of the year Neachdan digs the new well with wedge and oak maul in sleet and frost. His hands split at the knuckle and never close between one day's work and the next, and Sorcha rubs sheep-fat into the cracks each night.

events.title: Neachdan fills his tunic with the coloured stone
events.body: Breaking into the black seam, Neachdan finds pieces streaked gold, white, red-brown and silver, and one that holds every colour at once. Knowing no name or use for them, he judges them too beautiful to leave in the flooding shaft and carries them home against his chest.

events.title: Neachdan shelters as the storm breaks
events.body: A storm comes up the valley at dusk with a green-black sky. Neachdan caps the shaft and takes shelter under a crag above it rather than go back down into a flooding hole, and watches the light change to a thick yellow-brown before the sky breaks.

events.title: Neachdan finds the vein still burning under the rain
events.body: After the lightning strikes his capped shaft, Neachdan uncovers it to find the black seam awake along its whole face, breathing heat and a dark red flame that the driving rain cannot drown, only turn to a thin white smoke off its surface.

events.title: Neachdan weeps at the well's mouth
events.body: Kneeling at the shaft with his hands held over the burning vein, Neachdan feels warmth reach his split and aching knuckles for the first time since the winter began, and weeps at the well's edge in the storm.

events.title: The household gathers at the first hearth
events.body: Neachdan sets the carried coal on a swept ring of earth in his house. Sorcha, the boy Conall, and three younger children watch the first flame any household on Dia-thìr has ever kept, unsure at first whether it is dangerous.

events.title: The household learns the fire can be fed, and can die
events.body: As the first coal burns down to ash-grey crust, Neachdan breaks it open and finds it still glowing beneath. Sorcha feeds it dry heather from the bedding stack, and the household understands, in one night, that the fire must be fed or it will go out.

events.title: Sorcha burned by the fire
events.body: Feeding the fire a second time, Sorcha brushes her palm against the ash-grey crust of the coal, mistaking it for cold stone, and is burned across the base of her fingers. It is the first hurt any hearth on the island gives.

events.title: The household sets the rule of the stick
events.body: After Sorcha's burn, the household sets a rule kept ever after: the fire is fed with a stick's length between hand and flame, never with a bare palm. Sorcha teaches it to the younger children before dawn, showing them her reddened hand.

events.title: Neachdan says the fire must not go out
events.body: At dawn, with the storm spent and his household warm for the first time any of them can remember, Neachdan kneels by the fire with his hand on the cold earth and says it must not go out. Sorcha pledges to feed it as long as she has hands.

events.title: The well begun below the flat stone
events.body: Neachdan sets the first wedge on a rise a little east of the dead spring, where the older men of the valley say the rock runs true, and works through the dead of the year a hand's depth at a time.

events.title: The rock runs dark under the wedge
events.body: By the fifteenth day of the digging the shaft is over Neachdan's head and the rock has begun to run from grey to black, ringing under the maul instead of cracking clean.

events.title: Heather first fed to the fire
events.body: Sorcha lays a handful of dry bedding-heather against the failing coal on the first night, and the fire takes it faster and brighter than it took the stone; the household learns that the thing can be fed.

events.title: The first dawn by a fire
events.body: The household sits awake round the fire through the whole first night, and at grey dawn the children wake reddened by its glow instead of blued by the cold, for the first time in their lives.

events.title: Meat first set to the fire
events.body: A haunch of mutton hung too low over the hearth browns in the night, and the household wakes to a smell none of them has ever smelled; within a season meat is laid on stones heated at the fire's edge.

events.title: Ailbhe born by the hearth
events.body: A daughter is born to Neachdan and Sorcha so close to the fire that the women turn her aside for fear of a spark. She is the first child of the hill country to open her eyes by firelight rather than daylight alone. They name her Ailbhe.

events.title: The stone kept at the hearth's edge for meat
events.body: A flat stone is kept at the edge of the mason's hearth for the cooking of meat and nothing else, and the knowing of it goes out with every coal the household gives.

events.title: Teine a' Chlachair begged and given
events.body: A neighbouring household, its own hearth cold, comes asking for a coal of Teine a' Chlachair. Neachdan gives it freely and will not hear of any debt for it, telling his children that a fire withheld from a cold house is worse than a fire given away unthanked.

events.title: Fire first carried in a pot
events.body: The household hearth drowns in a night of driving rain. The boy Conall runs alone in the dark to the burning vein, scrapes a live coal into a clay water-pot banked round with cold ash, and carries it home to relight the fire. It is learned that fire need not stay where it is born.

events.title: The hearth dies in the wet spring
events.body: Three days of driven rain come through the thatch in the fifth spring after the lightning and put out the hearth in the black hour before dawn, with Neachdan from home.

events.title: Conall relights the hearth from the vein
events.body: Conall, eleven years old, runs barefoot through the rain to the burning vein with his mother's water-pot, scrapes a live piece into it, and brings the fire home to the dead hearth before his mother wakes.

events.title: The hut on the heather burns
events.body: A near household's fire, laid on packed heather, catches unseen from beneath and breaks into open flame under a heather roof. The family escapes with nothing saved. It is the first house lost to fire since the mason carried his home.

events.title: Conall's word: fire keeps to stone
events.body: Watching the burned household in its ruined yard, the young Conall says plainly what he has half understood since he was eleven: that a fire kept on stone can be trusted, and a fire laid on heather waits only for a moment's neglect to remember what it is.

events.title: Households begin laying stone under their fires
events.body: After the hut on the heather burns, the near hearths begin laying flat stones from the burn-bed beneath their fires, and the household that lost its roof rebuilds with a stone floor under its hearth.

events.title: Ailbhe first sent out with Poit an Teine
events.body: Ailbhe, still a girl, is sent alone two valleys off with a coal banked in ash in a clay pot, because her hands are steadier with a live coal than her brothers'.

events.title: Fire reaches the northern moor
events.body: Ailbhe, grown sure of the ground, carries a banked coal a full day's walk north to the edge of the moor at the limit of any household's grazing. Teine a' Chlachair, walked outward hearth by hearth, now burns in dozens of houses that were once each other's strangers.

events.title: Sorcha dies
events.body: Sorcha, who bore Ailbhe by the hearth and was herself the first to be burned by the fire her husband brought home, dies at Tobar dhìreach. The household keeps its fire fed through the mourning without letting it fall.

events.title: Neachdan dies
events.body: Neachdan, An Clachair, dies old by the hearth he lit from the burning vein, having asked once more to be carried to see the well-cut still burning. The household keeps the fire through the mourning as it has kept it every night since the lightning.

events.title: Conall's rule of the stone
events.body: At a gathering of the near hearths in the dark half of the year, Conall sets down standing what he has held since the burned hut: that fire kept from the mason's line should be laid on stone and never on packed heather. The near households take it as their own law.

events.title: Conall keeps the winter watch at the vein
events.body: Conall sits the dark half of every year on the two flat stones above the burning vein, and the valley's children learn not to go near them without an elder by.

events.title: Conall dies
events.body: Conall, who first carried Teine na Fèithe home in a water-pot as a boy, dies by the hearth in old age, with the vein in the well-cut still burning as it has burned since Oidhche an Dealanaich, unchanged through two of the mason's line.

events.title: The watch passed to Conall's son
events.body: Without ceremony, Conall's son takes up the watch of the burning vein his father and grandfather kept before him, sitting the dark half of the year on the two flat stones above the cut, understanding it is not his to let go out.

events.title: Tadhg's scorched stone
events.body: At the black well two valleys east, Tadhg holds up a dark-faced stone before a gathering and swears the lightning struck his own family's well, not the mason's. The mason's household hears of it and answers nothing, keeping the fire rather than the argument.

events.title: Ailbhe dies
events.body: Ailbhe, the fire-bearer, dies in her old age at the hearth she was born beside, having walked Teine a' Chlachair to more hearths than anyone had counted.

events.title: The young well's telling
events.body: An old woman of the young well to the south begins to tell, softly and without a stone to prove it, that her own mother saw the lightning fall into their well and not the mason's. The telling travels further than Tadhg's louder claim and outlasts it.

events.title: Three tellings held at once
events.body: The high valleys settle, without any household deciding it outright, into three tellings of where the lightning fell, held side by side and never set against each other. Only the scorched lip of the mason's own shaft still shows the truth of it, plainly, to anyone who walks to see.

events.title: Conall's son keeps the watch grown grey
events.body: Conall's son, grown grey at the watch his father left him, will not have the claims of the black well and the young well argued: the fire was walked to a hundred houses that do not care which valley the lightning chose.

events.title: Muirne born
events.body: A daughter is born at Tobar dhìreach, a great-granddaughter of Conall's line, and is given young to the household's hearth-keeper to be raised among the fire before she is raised among words. She is named Muirne.

events.title: Muirne takes up the watch of the well-cut
events.body: Not yet grown, Muirne begins to keep the winter watch over the burning vein as the keeper before her tires of the work, sitting the dark half of the year on the two flat stones as every keeper has sat since Conall.

events.title: Teine na Fèithe burns low
events.body: Through the years of Muirne's watch the glow in the broken vein fades winter on winter, unmarked by most of the valley, whose hundred hearths no longer need it, and marked only by the one keeper who sits with it in the cold.

events.title: Muirne marks Teine na Fèithe sinking
events.body: Keeping a private reckoning against her own memory, Muirne comes to see what no keeper before her has said aloud: that the glow in the well-cut grows a little lower with every winter, the vein burning down like any fire that is fed by nothing but itself.

events.title: Teine na Fèithe marked lower each winter
events.body: Muirne, sitting the dark half of the year on the flat stones, begins to keep a private reckoning of the glow in the well-cut against her memory of five winters before.

events.title: The last ember
events.body: In a wet spring of failed crops and standing water, Muirne sits out the last night of Teine na Fèithe in the rain and watches its pale glow go out, quietly, with no one else there to see Teine a' Chlachair die in the ground where it was struck.

events.title: Muirne refuses the digging
events.body: When talk turns to deepening the well-cut in hope of striking fire again, Muirne stands at the mouth of it and forbids the digging, saying the fire came out of the sky on one night only and is not a thing to be dug after in the ground.

events.title: The seed rots in the wet spring
events.body: The spring that finishes Teine na Fèithe is remembered also for rain that stands a hand deep in the low fields and rots the seed in the ground, so that hunger is abroad in the valleys.

events.title: Leac na Fèithe laid over the vein
events.body: The household levers a broad flat stone across the mouth of the mason's well-cut and packs its edge with turf, sealing the burnt vein from the weather and forbidding any water to be drawn near it again.

events.title: The new well cut
events.body: A stone's throw from the covered vein, the household cuts a fresh well that gives clean water from its first day, and it is this well, not the mason's old cut, that the household draws from from that day on.

events.title: Muirne tells the covering standing
events.body: Muirne tells the finding and the covering of the vein the same way every year, standing, until her telling is the one the household keeps unaltered: a wonder found, a wonder covered, and a well that gave water all the same.

events.title: Grandchildren sent out to Leac na Fèithe in Muirne's stead
events.body: Grown too slow for the winter walk, Muirne sends her grandchildren out to Leac na Fèithe to see that the turf at its edge still holds the rain out and that no bucket stands near it.

events.title: Muirne dies
events.body: Muirne dies at Tobar dhìreach in old age and is buried in the ground near the house with no coal or fire laid beside her, having already given the vein's fire, whole, back to the stone. The telling of Leac na Fèithe passes to her grandchildren.

events.title: A palm laid on the cold slab
events.body: The youngest of Muirne's grandchildren walks out to the covered stone in the dark half of the year and lays a bare palm on it, as she was taught, for what the stone once held.

events.title: Conn born to the upper valley
events.body: Conn is born to a herding household high up the Abhainn uaine, further inland and higher than any household of that kin cares to winter, the country from which the summer grazing is followed up onto the shrinking snowfields.

events.title: Conn trusted to choose the high ground
events.body: Grown to a young man, Conn reads the colour of the light on the high tops before dawn to judge whether the beasts want driving down, and is seldom wrong; the older herders of his kin begin letting him choose the summer ground himself.
